$comment: What a thing does at a temperature: where it melts, and where it boils, breaks down or turns straight to gas. Loam's own facts carry a melting point for only seven things, so the tube could not melt copper. Each row here is sourced on its own line. Melting is a change of STATE, not of substance: molten copper is still copper, and the engine keeps the thing's id and makes it a liquid. Where Loam has a recipe for the change (gold -> molten gold) Loam's recipe wins and these are not used.

$fields.range: low and high, for a mixture or alloy that has no single point
$fields.decomposes: it breaks down before it melts
$fields.sublimes: it goes straight from solid to gas
$fields.note: one plain sentence on why it is not a single clean number

acrylic_fibre.note: It degrades near 300 degrees instead of melting, which is why it is spun from solution.

actinium.note: The melting point is estimated and the boiling point extrapolated, as actinium is too scarce and radioactive to measure easily.

adenine.note: It decomposes between about 360 and 365 degrees.

adobe.note: Sun-dried mud brick, whose clay loses its water from about 550 degrees rather than melting.

agar.note: An agar gel sets below about 40 degrees but only melts again above 85 degrees.

agate.note: Banded chalcedony, which is quartz, so it melts where quartz does.

alanine.note: It sublimes rather than melting cleanly.

albite.note: The sodium end of the plagioclase feldspars, which melts lower than the calcium end.

alnico.note: Wikipedia gives this range for Alnico 3, and the other alnico grades differ with their mix.

alum.note: It melts at 92 to 95 degrees in its own water of crystallisation and then breaks down near 200.

alumina.note: Pure aluminium oxide, the workhorse of furnace linings and crucibles.

americium.note: Wikipedia marks the boiling point as calculated rather than measured.

amethyst.note: A purple variety of quartz, quoted as melting at about 1650 degrees give or take 75.

ammonium_bicarbonate.note: It breaks down to ammonia and carbon dioxide at about 42 degrees, which is why baker's ammonia smells.

ammonium_chloride.note: Sal ammoniac turns to vapour at about 338 degrees rather than melting quietly.

ammonium_nitrate.note: It melts at about 170 degrees and breaks down above 210.

andesite.note: Magma of this middling silica content is molten between about 850 and 1100 degrees.

anglesite.note: Lead sulfate melts at 1087 degrees while breaking down.

anhydrite.note: Calcium sulfate without its water melts at 1460 degrees.

anorthosite.note: Nearly all plagioclase feldspar, and the calcium-rich kind melts at about 1550 degrees while the sodium-rich kind melts far lower.

aragonite.note: The same calcium carbonate as calcite in another crystal form, and it too breaks down rather than melting.

arsenic.note: At ordinary pressure arsenic passes straight to vapour at about 614 degrees; melting it needs pressure.

asbestos.note: The fibres break down over a wide range rather than melting at one point.

atp.note: The disodium salt decomposes near 187 degrees instead of melting.

aventurine_quartz.note: Quartz flecked with glittering mica, so it melts where quartz does.

azurite.note: The blue copper carbonate breaks down to black copper oxide near 200 degrees instead of melting.

baking_soda.note: From about 50 degrees it breaks down into sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide instead of melting.

ballast.note: Rock of any ordinary kind is molten somewhere between about 700 and 1400 degrees, and this is a jumble of whatever rock was to hand.

barium_carbonate.note: It changes crystal form at 811 degrees and begins breaking down from about 1360.

baryte.note: Barium sulfate melts at 1580 degrees and starts breaking down just above.

basalt.note: Magma of this composition erupts at 1100 to 1200 degrees, and being a mixture of minerals it melts over a range.

bauxite.note: Bauxite is mostly aluminium hydroxide, which gives up its water near 300 degrees and leaves alumina behind.

beeswax.note: It darkens if heated much above 85 degrees.

berkelium.note: Both figures are for the beta form of the metal.

beryllium_copper.note: The alloy is pasty between its solidus at 866 C and its liquidus at 982 C.

beryllium_oxide.note: A refractory ceramic that melts above 2500 degrees.

beta_carotene.note: It decomposes at its melting point.

beta_ionone.note: The beta form, the one that smells of violets.

bha.note: A mixture of two closely related isomers, so it melts over a range.

bismuth_telluride.note: No boiling point is listed for this compound.

bleach.note: Household bleach is a watery solution; the pure pentahydrate crystals melt at 18 degrees and break down near 101.

blister_copper.note: Blister copper is about 98 percent copper, so it melts very close to copper's own point.

bloodstone.note: Green chalcedony spotted with red iron oxide, so it melts near where quartz does.

borax.note: Dry borax melts at 743 degrees, while the common crystals first lose their water and break down near 75.

borosilicate_glass.note: This is the softening point of Pyrex-type glass, which has no sharp melting point.

brass.note: Brass melts across a range that shifts with the proportion of copper to zinc.

breccia.note: Angular broken fragments cemented together, so it melts wherever the rock the pieces came from does.

brick.note: Fired clay has no true melting point: brick is fired at 900 to 1000 degrees and goes grey as it over-fires near 1300.

bronze.note: Wikipedia gives about 950 C, varying with the ratio of copper to tin, without stating the bounds of that variation.

butter.note: A mixture of fats, so it softens well before it melts.

caffeine.note: Dry caffeine sublimes below its melting point.

calcite.note: Calcium carbonate breaks down into quicklime and carbon dioxide above about 825 degrees instead of melting.

calcium_acetate.note: At 160 degrees it breaks down into chalk and acetone instead of melting.

calcium_carbide.note: The carbide used to make acetylene melts above 2100 degrees.

calcium_chloride.note: The dry salt melts at 772 to 775 degrees, while its hydrates break down far lower.

calcium_hydroxide.note: Slaked lime loses its water and breaks back down to quicklime near 580 degrees instead of melting.

californium.note: Wikipedia marks the boiling point as an estimation.

carbon.note: At ordinary pressure carbon sublimes at about 3900 kelvin rather than melting.

carbon_dioxide.note: At ordinary pressure it never melts: the solid sublimes straight to gas at minus 78 degrees.

carnelian.note: Chalcedony stained orange by iron, so it melts where quartz does.

cassiterite.note: The tin ore is tin dioxide, which melts at 1630 degrees, far above tin metal.

cast_iron.note: Carbon near 4.3 percent drops iron's melting point to about 1130 C, far below pure iron's 1538 C.

celestine.note: Strontium sulfate melts just above 1600 degrees.

cellulose.note: Cellulose chars and decomposes around 260 to 270 degrees instead of melting.

cement_meal.note: In the kiln the raw meal loses its carbon dioxide and sinters into clinker at about 1450 degrees instead of melting.

cerussite.note: Lead carbonate breaks down near 315 degrees instead of melting.

chalcedony.note: Quartz in microscopic fibres, so it melts where quartz does.

chalk.note: Heated limestone does not melt: above 840 degrees it gives off carbon dioxide and turns into quicklime.

chert.note: Microscopically fine quartz, so it melts about where ordinary quartz does.

chocolate.note: Chocolate melts just below body temperature because its cocoa butter does.

cholesterol.note: It decomposes near 360 degrees instead of boiling.

chromium_oxide.note: The green chromium oxide melts above 2400 degrees.

chrysoprase.note: Chalcedony coloured green by nickel, so it melts where quartz does.

cinnabar.note: The red form changes to black mercury sulfide at 344 degrees, and roasting in air drives off mercury vapour rather than melting it.

citric_acid.note: It starts to break down from about 175 degrees, so it has no clean boiling point.

citrine.note: A yellow variety of quartz, so it melts where quartz does.

clay.note: Clay does not melt: from about 550 degrees it gives up its water for good and turns into ceramic.

clinker.note: It is made by sintering, part-melting the kiln charge at about 1450 degrees.

cobalamin.note: It decomposes above 300 degrees instead of melting.

cobble.note: A cobble is whatever rock it happens to be, and ordinary rock is molten somewhere between about 700 and 1400 degrees.

columnar_basalt.note: It is ordinary basalt that cracked into columns as it cooled, so it melts over the same range.

conglomerate.note: Rounded pebbles cemented together, so it melts wherever the rock the pebbles came from does.

copernicium.note: Both figures are predictions carrying about ten degrees of uncertainty.

copper_cathode.note: Electrorefined cathode copper is refined copper, so it melts at copper's own point.

copper_oxide.note: The black copper oxide melts at 1326 degrees.

copper_sulfate.note: The blue crystals lose their water from about 110 degrees and the dry salt breaks down before it can melt.

copper_sulfide.note: The copper ore mineral melts at about 1130 degrees.

corundum.note: Crystalline aluminium oxide, one of the most heat-resistant common minerals.

cullet.note: Ordinary glass has no sharp melting point: it begins to soften from about 700 degrees.

curium.note: Wikipedia's infobox and body text disagree, the body giving 1344 C and 3556 C instead.

cysteine.note: It decomposes at its melting point.

cytosine.note: It decomposes between about 320 and 325 degrees.

dacite.note: Magma of this composition was measured at about 1050 degrees at Kilauea, and silica-rich magmas can be as cool as 800 degrees.

diamond.note: At ordinary pressure a diamond never melts: in air it catches light and burns away between about 690 and 840 degrees.

diorite.note: The coarse-grained twin of andesite, so it melts over the same middling range.

dunite.note: Almost pure olivine, which melts between 1200 and 1900 degrees depending on its iron content.

einsteinium.note: Wikipedia marks the boiling point as estimated.

enriched_uranium.note: Enrichment changes only the isotope mix, so enriched uranium metal melts and boils like ordinary uranium.

feldspar.note: A family rather than one mineral: the sodium feldspar albite melts at 1100 to 1120 degrees and the calcium-rich feldspars higher still.

fermium.note: The melting point is predicted, not measured, and no boiling point is known.

ferrovanadium.note: Wikipedia gives one figure although the vanadium content ranges from 35 to 85 percent.

flerovium.note: The melting point is a prediction with about fifty degrees of uncertainty, and no boiling point is given.

fluorite.note: Calcium fluoride melts at 1418 degrees, and molten fluorite is what gave fluxing its name.

folate.note: It decomposes at about 250 degrees rather than melting.

francium.note: Too little francium has ever existed at once to measure, so both figures are estimates.

fulgurite.note: It is sand already fused into glass by lightning, so it softens again near silica's melting point.

gabbro.note: The coarse-grained twin of basalt, with a liquidus near 1200 degrees.

galvanized_iron.note: Galvanised iron is steel under a zinc coat, so the coating runs at about 420 C while the steel beneath holds past 1500 C.

germanium_dioxide.note: Germanium dioxide melts at 1115 degrees, far below its silicon counterpart.

glass.note: Ordinary glass has no sharp melting point: it begins to soften from about 700 degrees.

glucose.note: This is the common alpha form; the beta form melts at about 150 degrees.

glutamic_acid.note: It decomposes at its melting point.

glutamine.note: It decomposes around 185 degrees rather than melting.

glycine.note: It decomposes at its melting point.

gneiss.note: Much the same minerals as granite, so it melts over granite's range, and water in the rock can bring that down to 650 degrees.

granite.note: A mixture of minerals, so it melts over a range rather than at one point, and water in the rock lowers it as far as 650 degrees.

graphite.note: Carbon has no melting point at ordinary pressure: it passes straight to vapour at about 3900 kelvin.

gravel.note: Rock of any ordinary kind is molten somewhere between about 700 and 1400 degrees, and this is a jumble of whatever rock was to hand.

guanine.note: It decomposes rather than melting and sublimes instead of boiling.

gypsum.note: Gypsum gives up its water as plaster long before this: it is the dry calcium sulfate that melts at 1460 degrees.

hematite.note: Iron oxide melts at this temperature, close to iron metal itself.

hydrochloric_acid.note: These are the values for pure hydrogen chloride, not for the watery acid in a bottle.

hydroxymethylfurfural.note: It forms when sugars break down, and it is a soft solid just above room temperature.

ice.note: Ice is simply solid water, so it melts at 0 degrees.

igneous_rock.note: Igneous rocks are frozen magma, and magma is molten anywhere from about 700 to 1400 degrees depending on its make-up.

inconel_625.note: This nickel superalloy melts between a solidus of 1290 C and a liquidus of 1350 C.

iodine.note: Iodine melts at about 114 degrees, though in an open tube it mostly sublimes into violet vapour.

jasper.note: Opaque quartz full of fine impurities, so it melts near where quartz does.

kaolin.note: The white china clay loses its water from about 550 degrees and will never again soften in water.

komatiite.note: An ultramafic lava so hot that it erupted at about 1600 degrees, far above ordinary basalt.

labradorite.note: A plagioclase feldspar part way between sodium albite, which melts near 1100 degrees, and calcium anorthite, which needs about 1550.

lactose.note: This is dry lactose; the usual monohydrate loses its water first.

laminations.note: Laminations are stacked strips of silicon electrical steel, which melts at about 1500 C.

lard.note: A mixture of fats, so it softens over a range that depends on the cut.

lawrencium.note: The melting point is predicted, not measured, and no boiling point is known.

lead_came.note: Came for stained glass is usually plain lead strip, so it melts at lead's own point.

lead_sulfide.note: Galena, the lead ore, melts at 1113 degrees, far above lead metal.

lignin.note: Wood, paper and other plant material char from about 350 degrees rather than melting.

lime.note: Slaked lime loses its water and breaks down rather than melting.

limestone.note: It does not melt at ordinary pressure: above about 825 degrees it breaks down into quicklime and carbon dioxide.

linoleic_acid.note: Reported values range from about minus 12 to minus 7 degrees.

litharge.note: The yellow lead oxide melts at 888 degrees, which is why it fluxes glass and glazes so readily.

lithium_carbonate.note: It melts at 723 degrees and begins to break down from about 1300.

livermorium.note: Wikipedia gives extrapolated bands rather than points, 364 to 507 C for melting and 762 to 862 C for boiling.

lodestone.note: Lodestone is magnetite that was magnetised in the ground, so it melts where magnetite does.

magnesium_chloride.note: The dry salt melts at 714 degrees, while the hydrated crystals break down on heating.

magnesium_oxide.note: One of the highest melting common oxides, which is why it lines furnaces.

magnesium_sulfate.note: Dry magnesium sulfate melts at 1124 degrees while breaking down, and Epsom salt crystals go at about 150.

magnetite.note: The magnetic iron oxide melts near 1600 degrees.

malachite.note: The green copper carbonate breaks down to black copper oxide near 200 degrees instead of melting.

maltose.note: This is the dry sugar; the monohydrate melts near 102 degrees.

manganese_dioxide.note: It breaks down near 535 degrees, losing oxygen instead of melting.

marble.note: Metamorphosed limestone, so it burns to quicklime and carbon dioxide instead of melting.

mendelevium.note: The melting point is predicted, not measured, and no boiling point is known.

metamorphic_rock.note: A class of rock rather than one material, and it melts only when it reaches the range magma occupies.

methionine.note: It decomposes at its melting point.

molybdenite.note: It breaks down at about 1185 degrees instead of melting.

monazite.note: The rare-earth phosphate melts somewhere between 1900 and 2100 degrees.

moraine.note: Rock of any ordinary kind is molten somewhere between about 700 and 1400 degrees, and this is a jumble of whatever rock was to hand.

moscovium.note: Both figures are predictions, as moscovium has only ever existed as a few atoms.

moss_agate.note: Agate with mossy mineral inclusions, so it melts near where quartz does.

mudstone.note: A hardened mud made of clay, which loses its water from about 550 degrees long before anything melts.

n_type.note: Silicon with a trace of phosphorus in it, which melts like ordinary silicon.

nak_alloy.note: The eutectic of 77 percent potassium and 23 percent sodium is liquid from -12.6 C up to 785 C.

neptunium.note: The boiling point is extrapolated from vapour pressure rather than measured.

nichrome.note: Wikipedia gives about 1400 C for C-grade nichrome, without stating bounds for other grades.

nickel_sulfate.note: The anhydrous salt breaks down above about 640 C instead of boiling, while the green hexahydrate melts at only 53 C.

nihonium.note: Both figures are predictions, as nihonium has only ever existed as a few atoms.

nobelium.note: The melting point is predicted, not measured, and no boiling point is known.

nylon.note: Nylon 6 melts near 220 degrees and nylon 6,6 near 265.

obsidian.note: A natural glass, so it softens over a range instead of melting at one point.

ochre.note: An earth pigment of clay stained with iron oxide, and the oxide itself melts at this temperature.

oganesson.note: Both figures are predictions, as oganesson has only ever existed as a few atoms.

olivine.note: Olivine melts somewhere between 1200 and 1900 degrees depending on how much iron it holds instead of magnesium.

overburden.note: Rock of any ordinary kind is molten somewhere between about 700 and 1400 degrees, and this is a jumble of whatever rock was to hand.

oxalate.note: The figure is for dry oxalic acid; the common dihydrate melts near 101 degrees.

p_type.note: Silicon with a trace of boron in it, which melts like ordinary silicon.

padparadscha.note: A pink-orange sapphire, so it melts where sapphire does.

paper.note: Wood, paper and other plant material char from about 350 degrees rather than melting.

pegmatite.note: A very coarse granite grown from a watery melt, which can stay liquid as low as 650 degrees where dry granite needs over 1200.

peridot.note: Gem olivine, quoted as melting between 1200 and 1900 degrees depending on its iron content.

peridotite.note: It is made mostly of olivine, which melts somewhere between 1200 and 1900 degrees depending on how much iron it holds.

perlite.note: It softens at 850 to 900 degrees, and the water trapped inside flashes to steam and puffs it up.

pet.note: Polyester fabric and drink bottles are both this plastic.

petalite.note: The lithium feldspar-like mineral melts at about 1350 degrees.

petrified_wood.note: Wood whose cells have been replaced by quartz, so it melts near where quartz does.

phosphorus.note: White phosphorus, the common form, melts at about 44 degrees.

phyllite.note: A slate taken a step further, so its sheet minerals break down from about 550 degrees before melting.

pig_iron.note: Pig iron's roughly 4 percent carbon drops its melting point to about 1130 C, which is why a blast furnace can tap it as a liquid.

polyacrylonitrile.note: It degrades near 300 degrees instead of melting, which is why it is spun from solution.

polycarbonate.note: It is glassy rather than crystalline, so it softens at this glass transition instead of melting sharply.

polyester.note: Polyester fabric and drink bottles are both this plastic.

polyethylene.note: A mixture of chain lengths, so it softens over a range.

porcelain.note: Porcelain is fired until it turns glassy at 1200 to 1400 degrees rather than melting at a set point.

porphyry.note: A texture rather than a single rock, so it melts wherever the magma it came from does.

potassium_acetate.note: It decomposes on further heating rather than boiling.

potassium_carbonate.note: Potash melts at 891 degrees and breaks down above that.

potassium_nitrate.note: Saltpetre melts at 334 degrees and gives off oxygen as it breaks down above 400.

potassium_nitrite.note: It decomposes as it melts and explodes near 537 degrees.

pp.note: The melting point depends on how regular the chains are.

proline.note: It decomposes over a range from about 205 to 228 degrees.

promethium.note: The boiling point is an estimate, as promethium has no stable isotope and is handled only in tiny amounts.

protactinium.note: Wikipedia flags the boiling point as uncertain.

pumice.note: Frothy volcanic glass of the silica-rich kind, so it softens over the range such lava is molten.

pvc.note: It softens over a wide range and starts to break down near 250 degrees.

pvdf.note: Above about 316 degrees it decomposes and gives off hydrogen fluoride.

pyrite.note: Fool's gold breaks down into iron sulfide and sulfur from about 540 degrees rather than melting.

pyrolusite.note: Manganese dioxide gives up oxygen and breaks down near 535 degrees rather than melting.

quartz.note: On the way up it turns into tridymite and then cristobalite, so two melting figures are quoted.

quartzite.note: Almost pure quartz welded together, so it melts about where silica does.

quicklime.note: Burnt lime is one of the most refractory oxides, melting above 2600 degrees.

radium.note: Wikipedia marks radium's melting point as disputed.

rail.note: A rail is rolled carbon steel, which softens over a range rather than melting at one point.

rhodochrosite.note: Manganese carbonate breaks down somewhere between 200 and 300 degrees rather than melting.

rhyolite.note: Lava of this silica-rich kind is molten anywhere from about 800 degrees upward, because it is a mixture and not one mineral.

rock.note: Rock is a mixture, so all that can honestly be given is the range in which ordinary rock is molten.

rock_candy.note: It does not melt cleanly: it starts breaking down below its melting point and turns into caramel.

rock_salt.note: Halite, common salt, melts at about 801 degrees into a clear liquid.

rose_quartz.note: A pink variety of quartz, so it melts where quartz does.

ruby.note: Ruby is corundum coloured red by chromium, so it melts where corundum does.

rust.note: Rust is a wet iron oxide: it dries out first, and the dry oxide melts at this temperature.

rutherfordium.note: Both figures are predictions, as rutherfordium has only ever existed as a few atoms.

rutilated_quartz.note: Quartz threaded with rutile needles, so it melts where quartz does.

rutile.note: Natural titanium dioxide, which melts well above 1800 degrees.

salicin.note: It decomposes near 240 degrees instead of boiling.

samarium.note: Wikipedia's infobox gives 1900 C for the boiling point while its body text gives 1794 C.

sand.note: Ordinary sand is mostly quartz grains, so it fuses near the melting point of silica.

sandstone.note: Mostly quartz grains, so it fuses near silica's melting point, though the cement between the grains gives way first.

sapphire.note: Sapphire is corundum coloured by iron and titanium, and melts just above 2000 degrees.

schist.note: A crustal rock that begins to melt in patches once it is hot and wet, and needs over 1200 degrees to melt dry.

scree.note: Rock of any ordinary kind is molten somewhere between about 700 and 1400 degrees, and this is a jumble of whatever rock was to hand.

sediment.note: Rock of any ordinary kind is molten somewhere between about 700 and 1400 degrees, and this is a jumble of whatever rock was to hand.

sedimentary_rock.note: A class of rock rather than one material, so only the broad range in which rock melts can be given.

selenium.note: Grey selenium melts at about 221 degrees.

serine.note: It decomposes at its melting point.

shale.note: A layered clay rock, so it first loses the water locked in its clay from about 550 degrees.

silica.note: Pure silicon dioxide melts at this temperature, which is why it is the backbone of glass and refractories.

silica_sand.note: Sand sorted for its quartz content, so it fuses close to silica's own melting point.

silicon.note: Silicon melts at 1414 degrees because its covalent network has to be broken apart.

silicon_carbide.note: It decomposes at that temperature instead of melting cleanly.

silicon_dioxide.note: Sand is mostly silica, which melts only at white heat.

silt.note: Rock of any ordinary kind is molten somewhere between about 700 and 1400 degrees, and this is a jumble of whatever rock was to hand.

silver_carbonate.note: It begins breaking down at about 120 C, before its 218 C melting point is reached.

slate.note: Metamorphosed mudstone, so the clay minerals in it break down from about 550 degrees before melting.

smithsonite.note: Zinc carbonate breaks down near 140 degrees, leaving zinc oxide behind.

smoky_quartz.note: A brown variety of quartz, so it melts where quartz does.

soap.note: Hard soap is largely sodium stearate, which melts over this range.

sodium_acetate.note: The anhydrous salt; the trihydrate melts at about 58 degrees.

sodium_carbonate.note: Dry soda ash melts at 851 degrees, which is why it is added to glass batches as a flux.

sodium_hydroxide.note: Caustic soda melts at 323 degrees into a liquid that attacks glass.

sodium_nitrate.note: Chile saltpetre melts at 308 degrees and breaks down above 380.

sodium_sulfate.note: The dry salt melts at 884 degrees, while the crystals melt in their own water at about 32.

solder.note: Soft solders are a whole family melting anywhere from 90 to 450 C, and the single figure here is common 60/40 tin-lead.

sorbate.note: Potassium sorbate decomposes as it melts.

stainless_steel.note: Stainless steel melts over a range that depends on which alloy it is.

stearin.note: A mixture of hard fats, so it melts over a range.

steel.note: Carbon steel softens over a range rather than at one point, and this range is the one Wikipedia gives for A36 structural steel.

stone.note: Stone is whatever rock it was cut from, and ordinary rock is molten somewhere between about 700 and 1400 degrees.

sugar.note: It does not melt cleanly: it starts breaking down below its melting point and turns into caramel.

sulfur.note: Brimstone melts at about 115 degrees to a blood-red liquid and boils at 445.

sunstone.note: A plagioclase feldspar flecked with copper or iron, melting somewhere between albite's 1100 degrees and anorthite's 1550.

synephrine.note: This is the natural form; the mixed form melts near 184 degrees.

tannin.note: Tannins char rather than melt: tannic acid breaks down above 200 degrees.

tarnish.note: The black tarnish on silver is silver sulfide, which melts at 836 C.

tartaric_acid.note: This is the natural form; the mixed form melts near 206 degrees.

tempered_clay.note: A clay body mixed ready for the kiln; from about 550 degrees its clay loses its water for good.

tennessine.note: The melting point is predicted only as a band from 350 to 550 C, and the boiling point is also a prediction.

thymine.note: It decomposes near 335 degrees instead of boiling.

tigers_eye.note: Quartz that has replaced fibrous asbestos, so it melts where quartz does.

tin_dioxide.note: Tin dioxide melts at 1630 degrees, hundreds of degrees above tin metal.

tin_silver_solder.note: The tin-silver eutectic melts at a single point rather than over a range.

titanium_dioxide.note: A very refractory white oxide, used as pigment long before it ever melts.

titanium_nitride.note: No boiling point is listed for this ceramic.

trans_fat.note: Elaidic acid, the commonest trans fat, melts at 45 degrees, well above its natural twin oleic acid.

travertine.note: A banded freshwater limestone, so it calcines to quicklime rather than melting.

tuff.note: Packed volcanic ash of whatever magma erupted, so only the broad range of lava temperatures can be given.

tungsten_carbide.note: Wikipedia gives the melting point as a band from 2785 to 2830 C.

urea.note: It decomposes on further heating instead of boiling.

valine.note: It decomposes at its melting point.

vitamin_e.note: Vitamin E is an oil that only sets just above freezing point.

waste_rock.note: Rock of any ordinary kind is molten somewhere between about 700 and 1400 degrees, and this is a jumble of whatever rock was to hand.

wax.note: Paraffin wax is a mixture of hydrocarbons, so it softens and melts over a range.

wood.note: Wood, paper and other plant material char from about 350 degrees rather than melting.

wrought_iron.note: Wrought iron was always worked hot rather than melted, since with almost no carbon it melts as high as pure iron.

zinc_chloride.note: It melts at 290 degrees and boils by 732.

zinc_oxide.note: It melts near 1974 degrees while also breaking down.

zinc_sulfide.note: It passes straight from solid to vapour near 1850 degrees.

zircon.note: It breaks down into zirconia and silica at about 1540 degrees rather than melting cleanly.
